newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania lek slides in market, rates increased.
newsitem.headline: Albania lek slides in market, rates increased.

text.p: The Albanian lek is taking a beating in Tirana's thriving, open-air currency market as people rush to buy dollars following the dramatic disintegration of pyramid investment schemes.

With the lek down 30 percent since the start of the year, state banks have introduced tight foreign exchange curbs and even the crowds of money dealers in Tirana's unofficial street market are reluctant to sell hard currencies.
"If you think I'm going to sell dollars today you must be crazy," said Nardi, one of about 500 dealers who hawk for trade along the dusty streets outside Albania's central bank.

In the space of one hour early on Friday, the street rate slipped to 133 from 127 -- it stood at 104 at the start of 1997. The official bank rate was set at 128 lek to the dollar on Friday but only tiny transactions were being allowed.
In a bid to shore up the currency, the central bank raised its 12-month deposit rates 400 basis points to 23 percent.
Finance Minister Ridvan Bode said the lek's slide had nothing to do with the state of the economy.

"What is actually happening in the market nowadays is a simple psychological effect," he told state television. "The bid/ask ratio does not reflect the real exchange rate between the lek and the dollar."
But money dealers warned that the lek would fall further unless state banks increased foreign currency trading.
"Unless the bank intervenes it will reach 150 to the dollar next week," said Muli, another street dealer.
A dealer at a state bank said selling of dollars was limited "because officials are worried about panic in the monetary market."

Economists believe more than $1 billion is tied up in the pyramid saving schemes, which started to fail at the end of last year, leaving many people in Europe's poorest country facing ruin and sparking social unrest.
"There are rumours about devaluation and hyper-inflation and even some of the food shops are starting to accept just hard currencies," Muli added.

Other types of shops are happy to accept any currency, even the lek, just to keep business going. "I have only sold four pairs of shoes all week and will go bankrupt," said Arben, who owns a small shop close to the money market.

The central bank is believed to have around $270 million in foreign reserves, while the street dealers say their own stash of dollars is running short, having sold over $1 million at the start of the week alone.
The only people doing roaring trade on the streets were the men selling visa application forms for the United States at 50 cents a go. One dealer said he was selling 600 a day.

Other people came to the money changers to offer them their privatisation certificates in state companies, which Albania's right-wing government handed out last year to encourage the idea of share ownership and the free market.
The purple certificates have a face value of 40,000 lek, but pensioners were being offered just four percent of that.
